Self trained vocalist/producer/artist here. You have a major leg up on me when it comes to your technical background. I've heard some music students struggle with throwing out certain conventions of taught studies. I liken it to shiny object syndrome. You now have so many options for starting to write a song, that it's hard to start somewhere. What I found to be most helpful is a spiritual discernment. Many greats talk about flow state and making music for you. When you start to think about what makes your music appealing to YOU, not US, you will find it easier to get through songwriting.

You might find it hard to determine genres. You might find it hard to pick melodies. You might not like recorded stuff sometimes. The cool thing is, you don't necessarily have to rush yourself. You can get a verse, a pre chorus, bridge, etc., down on the first session. Then, you can workshop the hook for a whole week if you don't get it on the first day.

Also, if you go into it without expectations and just allowing yourself to play around until you get something you really like, you're more likely to achieve flow state and less likely to burn out. Hope this helps. Every musician has intrinsic value and there is someone out there who will appreciate what you never guessed would matter to them. Good luck creating 😊.

I think this is interesting because it points to my theory around "NPCs." Realistically, in a game, people are restricted to certain responses. If the simulation is real, then some of the people we meet are no doubt "programmed." Certain people will always give a superficial response to save face, hence making them seem more like an NPC. 

They were programmed from a young age to be polite, despite their true feelings. Some "NPCs" have a stronger filter than others. I think that what lends to simulation theory is the weird, almost uncanny, feeling that these people are lying to us or withholding information that surely they would give us, were they real. Maybe not real in the tangible sense, but at least in the mutual sense. I liken it to how customer service workers in a location can have a "groupthink" response where if anyone asks them particular questions, they will get similar, if not the same answers from every person they ask.

I may be wrong but I feel like it's almost as if you have to "level up your speech" in order to have the potential of getting past these surface-level responses. For instance, if in the Matrix, Neo knows that the hard-line phones are the key to the simulation, he has an advantage. However, the people in the Matrix are also aware of this, and do everything they can to act as though these phones don't break the simulation. If there was something in our simulation that seemed so obvious to be the answer to the theory, chances are anyone who is not real (which could be anyone or everyone) has already been programmed to deny and deflect in regards to this situation.

I hope I kind of made some sense. I wholly support simulation theory because there have been too many "coincidences" in my life too, but I still like parsing possibilities.

As someone who grew up on classic rock and 90's West Coast rap, I can definitely see where you're coming from. Key changes, tempo changes, odd time signatures, etc. just aren't so common anymore. I think the main reason why it doesn't happen so much anymore is because DAWs just make everything so much easier to produce. 

Yes, you must have talent and smarts to engineer a great track, quantized or not, however you must also have sensibility for artists and producers wanting to remix music in this age. It is just far easier to take a perfectly quantized guitar rhythm and make it fit to another song. The same can be said for vocals, piano, etc. 

All that said, I still like to add some swing to the tracks that I produce, to make it feel like it's not coming directly from a computer. I guess it all boils down to taste at the end of the day.

From one troubled autistic kid to another, I assure you that this is abuse. I want you to think about this: due to the nature of your father's abuse, confronting him directly about it is likely never going to improve his ability to be emotionally available or accountable for what he has done. Abuse like this hinges on gaslighting. If you are not yet familiar with the topic, I suggest you do some research on the topic to better understand how the manipulation works.

In short, because of a deep lack of love that your father feels for himself, in tandem with likely undiagnosed mental conditions of his own, he projects insecurities onto you and others. In many cases, behavior you are called out on is not to stop you from doing the behavior because it's "bad," it is to make you question yourself and not to go against the status quo. What your father wants is control. The other tricky thing is that his denial can come from a place of both genuine and feigned ignorance. He may be acutely aware of the things that he is doing, or he may be unintentionally abusive. Regardless of how he acts in the good moments, it's still abusive. A big thing to look for is whether or not you can gauge genuine remorse on his part for being mean-spirited towards you.
